clue.text: Hardy hero taking good puff before award

indicators.note: the hero taking something means he takes it into himself, holding it inside his name
before places the advert piece at the front, ahead of the hero with his added letter

blocks.note: a puff is a promotional plug, an advert
Jude the Obscure is the hero of Thomas Hardy's last novel
G is the standard abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A Thomas Hardy character smokes a fine puff before receiving a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: Jude takes G inside to become JUDGE, and the advert goes in front: AD + JUDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To adjudge is to grant formally by a ruling, so a court can adjudge damages, which is to award them.

clue.text: Agree to a rise, we're told

indicators.note: something we are told reaches us by ear, so the word for a rise is judged by its sound

blocks.note: an ascent is a climb or rise

explanation.surface: Someone consents to a pay rise, or so the rumour goes.
explanation.definitionFit: To assent is to express consent or approval, the verb used of a monarch signing a bill into law.

clue.text: River ordinance incorporated within the month

indicators.note: incorporated within says one piece is enclosed inside the body of another

blocks.note: Jan is the short form of January
ORD is a dictionary abbreviation of ordinance

explanation.surface: A regulation about rivers is folded into this month's business.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jordan flows from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea, famous as the river of baptism.

clue.text: Where scullions knew their place

blocks.note: surface reading: kitchen servants behaved with proper humility
setter's reading: the literal place servants worked and lived, below the family's floors

explanation.walkthrough: Knowing your place usually means social deference; here it is a physical location, the servants' quarters of a grand house.
explanation.definitionFit: In big Victorian houses kitchens and servants' halls sat on the lower floor, so servants as a class were called that.

clue.text: Gain the same standard uniform

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, to match or reach the level of
second meaning: an adjective, identical throughout

explanation.surface: Achieving parity in what soldiers wear on parade.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means to match a record or rival; as an adjective it means even, alike, consistent.

clue.text: Subsequent article left on one side

blocks.note: subsequent means coming afterwards
a is the indefinite article
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece written afterwards was abandoned and put aside.
explanation.definitionFit: Lateral describes something positioned at the side, sideways rather than front or back.

clue.text: Amusing items in the auction?

definitions.note: a whimsical phrase: lots are auction items, so fun ones are lots of fun

blocks.note: first meaning: highly entertaining
second meaning, read whimsically: lots are the items under the hammer, and these are the entertaining ones

explanation.surface: Comic odds and ends turning up at a saleroom.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday phrase means very enjoyable, while lots is also the auctioneer's word for separate items offered for sale.

clue.text: Utterly wrong tense

indicators.note: utterly is read as in an uttered way, spoken out, so the word for wrong is judged by its sound

blocks.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: Someone has used entirely the wrong verb tense.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech TORT and TAUT sound the same. Utterly looks like an intensifier but signals speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Taut and tense both describe a rope or nerves pulled tight, stretched with no slack.

clue.text: Do a dry run? Here goes - bottom's down!

indicators.note: goes suggests the letters go off and break up, so they are rearranged
in a down entry, down places the next piece at the lower end, after the rest

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be shuffled
arse is British slang for the backside

explanation.surface: A performer announces a practice run and drops their trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here goes' reads as a nervous announcement, but goes works on here. Arse is British slang for bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehearse is to practise a performance beforehand, which is what a dry run means.

clue.text: Doctor Dylan's MA presented to Don Giovanni

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the following letters are altered in order

blocks.note: the letters of the name and degree, used as they stand

explanation.surface: A doctor named Dylan receives his master's degree at a performance of Mozart's opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor looks like a title for Dylan but is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Don Giovanni, the seducer in Mozart's opera, is the archetypal womaniser, a man who charms women.

clue.text: Verrucas repelled Jack

indicators.note: something repelled is driven back the way it came, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: verrucas are warts on the foot

explanation.surface: Someone called Jack fought off his verrucas.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Straw was a Labour Home Secretary and also a leader of the 1381 Peasants' Revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname completes a famous name: Jack Straw, the British politician and the rebel of 1381.

clue.text: Virgin is indifferent?

blocks.note: first meaning: pristine, never handled or used
second meaning: not emotionally moved

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark tempts a link between chastity and coldness; the two words are separate senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both pristine, never handled, like virgin snow, and emotionally unmoved by something.

clue.text: The outcome of a big splash out o-on flash do?

indicators.note: the outcome of is what results once the following letters are worked on and reshaped
out suggests the letters are knocked out of their order and rearranged

blocks.note: the letters as printed, stammer included

explanation.surface: A stammering guest wonders what a lavish party will lead to.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter in o-on supplies the extra O the fodder needs.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical deluge of Genesis, which drowned the world, is humorously described as an enormous splash of water.

clue.text: Rubbed shoulders, maybe, with state elder

blocks.note: Mass is the abbreviation for Massachusetts
elder people are aged

explanation.surface: Someone mingled socially with a senior statesman.
explanation.walkthrough: Rubbed shoulders looks like the idiom for mixing socially, but it means literally kneaded someone's shoulders; maybe flags that as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Massaging shoulders is one instance of rubbing a body part, hence the maybe.

clue.text: The French left Munich man in time to reach Burgundy

indicators.note: left is read as departed, so those letters go missing
in places one piece inside the remainder

blocks.note: la is French for the, feminine
Neville Chamberlain signed the 1938 Munich Agreement
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: French people abandon a Munich man who must travel to Burgundy in time.
explanation.walkthrough: Left looks like a direction but means departed. Chamberlain was the British prime minister who signed the 1938 Munich Agreement with Hitler.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambertin is a celebrated grand cru red wine from the Côte de Nuits, so it is a Burgundy.

clue.text: Sound of a ship's cannon?

blocks.note: first meaning: an inlet or strait of water
second meaning, read whimsically: a weapon carried at sea

explanation.walkthrough: Sound looks like noise from a gun; it is a stretch of water, and the cannon is a weapon, an arm, belonging to the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A sound is a narrow inlet of the sea, and arms means weapons, so naval guns are arms used at sea.

clue.text: One's taken up by the painter with a handshake

definitions.text: One's taken up by the painter with a handshake

blocks.clueFragment: taken up by the painter with a handshake
blocks.note: surface reading: an artist accepts an offer and shakes hands on it
setter's reading: a tool an artist picks up to stop the hand shaking

explanation.walkthrough: Handshake suggests sealing a deal; read it as a hand that shakes, which this rest supports.
explanation.definitionFit: This light padded rod is held across the canvas by artists to steady the brush hand during fine work.

clue.text: Airline cuts revealing sums of spare cash

blocks.note: BA is British Airways
to lance is to cut open, as a boil

explanation.surface: An airline makes cuts and discovers it has surplus money.
explanation.definitionFit: Balances are the amounts left over in accounts after spending, remaining money not yet used.

clue.text: 6 is underlined

definitions.note: the answer to 6 down, an adjective meaning tense

blocks.note: first meaning: the answer to 6 down, tense or tight
second meaning: emphasised

explanation.definitionFit: Stressed describes someone anxious and tight-strung, and also a point emphasised, given extra weight.

clue.text: One is opposed to bishop greeting trade union? What a bloomer!

blocks.note: someone anti something is against it
RR is Right Reverend, a bishop's title
hi is a greeting
NUM is the National Union of Mineworkers

explanation.surface: A bishop snubs a union delegation, and someone exclaims at the blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloomer sounds like a gaffe but is a flowering plant. The NUM is the British miners' union.
explanation.definitionFit: The antirrhinum, or snapdragon, is a garden flower, so it is a plant that blooms.

clue.text: Beef and game

blocks.note: first meaning: a complaint
second meaning: a wild bird that is shot

explanation.surface: Two kinds of meat on a menu.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like meats; beef is slang for a complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: A grouse is a gripe, which beef also means in slang, and it is a moorland bird hunted for sport.

clue.text: Grant is held up by student peccadilloes

indicators.note: held means the answer is contained within the following words
in a down entry, up means the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters straddling the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A student's grant is delayed because of minor misdeeds.
explanation.walkthrough: Grant looks like a student's funding but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To grant a point is to concede or acknowledge it, which is what accepting it means.

clue.text: See 12
Unbalanced and unhappy star takes back TV trophy, sick at heart

indicators.note: an unhappy thing is out of sorts, so its letters are disturbed
takes means the shuffled word holds the next piece inside it
back means the trophy is read backwards
at heart keeps only the central part of the word

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be shuffled
the Emmy is the US television award
the two middle letters

explanation.surface: A disturbed celebrity withdraws an award and feels ill.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed trophy goes inside the shuffled star, splitting it after its second letter, and the heart of sick is tacked on at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Asymmetric means lacking symmetry, with the two sides unequal, which is a sense of unbalanced.

clue.text: Elated, magnetic? Get away!

indicators.note: the instruction to get away sends those letters off, out of the word

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letters to be taken out

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled and charismatic is told 'Get away!' in disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get away!' reads as an exclamation of surprise but tells you to strip those letters from magnetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Manic describes wild, excited high spirits, an overly elevated mood.

clue.text: Prima dona taking into her veins something impounded by state prosecutor

indicators.note: something impounded is locked up inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a DA is a US district attorney
IV, intravenous, means into a vein, as with a drip

explanation.surface: An opera star taking drugs intravenously is caught by the prosecutor.
explanation.definitionFit: A diva is the leading female opera singer, which is what prima donna means; the clue spells it dona.

clue.text: Spaniard is given a part: the continental Scotsman?

blocks.note: an actor cast is given a role
il is the Italian for the
Ian is a typically Scottish first name

explanation.surface: A Spanish actor receives a role playing a European Scot.
explanation.walkthrough: Continental the means a European word for the, here Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: A Castilian is a native of Castile, the central region of Spain, so a type of Spaniard.

clue.text: "Ne plus ultra", so far as this region goes!

definitions.text: "Ne plus ultra", so far as this region goes!

blocks.note: surface reading: the peak of perfection, the very best

blocks.clueFragment: so far as this region goes
blocks.note: setter's reading: Latin for nothing further beyond, the edge of the known world

explanation.walkthrough: Ne plus ultra usually means the ultimate in quality; read literally it means no further, which describes the classical end of the world.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient geographers named a land in the far north as the most remote region, Ultima Thule, beyond which nothing lay.

clue.text: Blue wine is a washout

blocks.note: feeling blue is feeling down
sack is an old word for a dry white sherry-style wine

explanation.surface: A disappointing wine turns out to be a flop.
explanation.definitionFit: A sad sack is a hopeless, inept person, a failure, which is what a washout means.

clue.text: In hall, grand parties promenade ¿ every one of them

definitions.text: In hall, grand parties promenade ¿ every one of them

blocks.note: surface reading: guests at a smart party stroll about a hall
setter's reading: the answer pairs with each of hall, grand, parties and promenade to make a familiar phrase

explanation.walkthrough: The four words each combine with the answer: a hall, a grand piano, parties of performers, and the Proms series.
explanation.definitionFit: The word forms a known compound with each listed term, and all relate to a musical performance before an audience.
